claims.text: The initial W–Cu composite consists of tungsten particles dispersed in a copper matrix.
The proposed intervention is alloying the Cu matrix with 2–5 wt% Ag.
Adding 2–5 wt% Ag to the Cu phase will increase the thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
The Ag-modified composite will retain mechanical durability relative to an otherwise comparable Ag-free W–Cu composite.
The Ag-modified composite will retain irradiation resistance relative to an otherwise comparable Ag-free W–Cu composite.
Ag atoms substitute into the Cu matrix.
Ag substitution may reduce grain-boundary scattering in the Cu matrix.
Ag substitution may reduce W–Cu interface scattering.
Ag addition improves the intrinsic thermal conductivity of the Cu matrix.
Ag addition increases Cu-matrix electrical and thermal conductivity by reducing impurity and defect scattering.
Ag is ductile and does not embrittle Cu at the proposed concentration.
Low Ag concentrations do not significantly alter the Cu matrix's response to neutron damage.
The Ag-modified composite will have at least 10% higher thermal conductivity than the baseline W–Cu composite.
The hardness and toughness of the Ag-modified composite will remain within 5% of baseline values.
The irradiation resistance of the Ag-modified composite will remain within 5% of the baseline value.
Keeping the Ag fraction below 5 wt% avoids phase separation.
The predicted effect holds at temperatures up to 600°C, for W volume fractions of 30–70%, and at fusion-relevant neutron doses below 1 dpa.
Ag segregation or precipitation could adversely affect mechanical properties or irradiation resistance.

contradictions.description: The intervention permits 2–5 wt% Ag, including 5 wt%, whereas the boundary states that the Ag fraction must remain below 5 wt%.
The claimed validity boundary is irradiation below 1 dpa, while the experiment permits irradiation up to 1 dpa; an endpoint of exactly 1 dpa lies outside the stated strict boundary.
